subject: Public health
summary: Key principles for preventing disease in East African hospitals: sanitation, vaccination, nutrition, surveillance, and rapid response. Clinicians must integrate public health into bedside care and ward management.

sections.p: Public health focuses on population health, disease prevention, and health promotion. In low‑resource settings, it is essential for reducing preventable admissions and improving outcomes.
b: Disease burden driven by sanitation, nutrition, and infectious agents
Health systems rely on surveillance, vaccination, and basic hygiene

sections.h: Features of the Public Health System
sections.p: A functional public health system includes surveillance, vaccination programmes, water and sanitation, nutrition, and health education.
b: Surveillance: case reporting, trend analysis
Vaccination: routine and outbreak control
Water & sanitation: safe drinking water, latrine coverage
Nutrition: iron‑deficiency prevention, complementary feeding

sections.h: Transmission and Life Cycle of Key Preventable Diseases
sections.p: Many common infections spread via contaminated water, food, or vectors. Understanding their life cycles guides control measures.
b: Water‑borne: cholera, typhoid
Food‑borne: hepatitis A, E
Vector‑borne: malaria, dengue

sections.p: Public health failures lead to outbreaks of diarrhoea, typhoid, malaria, and nutritional deficiencies.
b: Diarrhoeal disease: high morbidity in children
Typhoid fever: fever, abdominal pain, rose spots

sections.p: Clinical assessment combined with simple tests is often sufficient.
b: History of water source, sanitation
Physical signs: dehydration, pallor

sections.p: Treat the cause, provide supportive care, and implement preventive measures.
b: Antibiotics for bacterial infections
ORS for dehydration
Antimalarials for confirmed malaria

t.b: Administer 1–2 L per day based on severity

sections.p: Clinicians must link bedside findings to public health interventions.
b: Ask about water source in diarrhoea
Check vaccination status in febrile illness
Advise iron supplementation in anaemic children

sections.p: Some conditions mimic public health problems but have different management.
b: Typhoid vs. malaria: both febrile but differ in stool culture and malaria test

sections.p: Low sensitivity of tests and false negatives can delay treatment.
b: Rapid malaria test may miss low parasitaemia
Stool culture may be negative if antibiotics used

sections.p: Urgent referral for severe dehydration, shock, or haemorrhage.
b: Signs of shock: tachycardia >120/min, hypotension
Severe anaemia: Hb <7 g/dL with tachycardia

faq.q: What is the most common preventable cause of hospital admissions in Kenya?
faq.a: Diarrhoeal disease due to poor sanitation and unsafe water.

faq.q: Which vaccine is essential for children in East Africa?
faq.a: Oral cholera vaccine and routine immunisations (BCG, measles, polio).

faq.q: How do you manage a child with suspected iron‑deficiency anaemia?
faq.a: Give oral iron supplements, counsel on iron‑rich diet, and investigate for ongoing blood loss.

exam: A 5‑year‑old presents with fever and abdominal pain; stool culture is negative. What is the next step? — Consider typhoid; repeat culture or use Widal test; start empiric antibiotics if high suspicion.
A patient with suspected malaria has a negative rapid test but high clinical suspicion. What do you do? — Repeat test, consider microscopy, treat empirically if severe.
A ward has an outbreak of diarrhoea. What public health measure should you implement first? — Ensure safe drinking water, promote hand hygiene, isolate cases.
Why is iron supplementation avoided in a patient with haemoglobinuria? — Risk of worsening renal damage; investigate underlying cause first.
What is the key difference between typhoid fever and malaria on physical exam? — Typhoid may have rose spots; malaria often has splenomegaly.
When is oral cholera vaccine indicated? — During cholera outbreaks or in high‑risk communities.
